utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Madam Registrar. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Everyone is here, except Mr. Bourgon. The Prosecution team is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. I understand there are some preliminaries. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In an effort to help shed some more light on this issue of the dates and these printouts, I spoke with the person that had more knowledge about this in our team and we have identified what we believe are the different reports that were sent out on the 14th with the various numbers and headings that will, I think, help resolve the issue, if this witness remembers them and recognises them. I hate to say I've not gone over this stuff with him and asked him about it. That was for the bigger -- the overall witness who is coming second. So if he can't talk about it, the other witness can. But we can try to ask him and see if he remembers these issues and, if he can, then it may help resolve it. But I think you'll just see from the face of the documents that it's pretty obvious that some of the concerns and questions made sense yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you so much, Mr. McCloskey. Any other preliminaries? Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we move to private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, Witness, everyone. I'm going to be referring to a new series of documents which we have marked P02312, if we could -- everyone should have the physical packet on that to refer to. It's B/C/S but I'm going to try to stick to just numbers and things so we won't need to go into too much English at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, I have a bit of a surprise for you this afternoon because I have this exhibit for you as well and it -- it's not something that I've shown you before and I've written in ink P 02312 on it and if you could just study it a bit, especially -- not -- not -- I don't need to you look so much in the content of the various intercepts right now but if you could go through the different headings up in the left-hand corner, especially the numbers. And the first question, let me ask you, is: As we look up in the left-hand corner, it says, "STR. POV. BR." Can you -- can you tell me what that -- what that means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, sir. First of all, good afternoon to you. I was -- I'm a bit absent minded today. Can you please put your question again? I was not with you all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Looking up in the left-hand corner of this first page, about four lines down, there is the abbreviation "STR. POV. BR." Do you know what those abbreviations stand for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I saw that my client had some difficulty, Your Honour. He called the usher over. I don't know what it is. I don't think it's been solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Gvero, what's the problem? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] I cannot see the transcript on the monitor and the accused's microphone is not on so the interpreter missed the second part of the -- I don't have either the transcript or the e-court on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will given you all the assistance required. In the meantime, perhaps, as Judge Kwon is suggesting, if you can move closer to General Pandurevic, you can try and follow from his while we fix yours. I'm sure you wouldn't mind, Mr. Pandurevic. THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Thank you for your assistance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it being taken care of? All right. Okay. Thank you. We can proceed. Mr. McCloskey, perhaps it's the case of putting the question again the third time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, this abbreviation, "STR. POV. BR."?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I apologise to the Trial Chamber. I did not adapt to the courtroom right away. Now I'm ready to answer the question. I had some noise in my head phones. I don't know what this noise is about. The abbreviation that you are asking me about stands for strictly confidential, and the document bears a number, so this is something that you will find on strictly confidential documents under certain numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, and if you could take a minute to look at the other documents underneath the one on the top, sometimes the documents are one or two or more pages, but if you could go to the next document that has a heading and a strictly confidential number, you will notice that that number begins with 02. So the first one was 01, the second one was 02, if we look at the next document in line, it's 03, and then 04, so on. Now, with that in mind, we -- let's go back to the first page, and after 01 we see a slash and we see five numbers that can be read in a number of different ways. Do you know what those five numbers reflect? For example, if they are read in the 14, 7, 95, what would that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That number can be found in every report. I can only assume that this was the key for that day but this is just my assumption. We can see that the report was sent on a certain date and that they follow a sequence, the first one, the second one, the third one, which means that on that day, there were a number of reports sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Is it possible that that 14, 7, 95, is the 14th day of July 1995? Because as I -- as I look at all of these, 1 through some 13, 14, 15, I see the same numbers, 1, 4, 7, 9, 5.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that they tally with the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So if we have -- we have 16 numbered reports, all with the slash and the 14, 7, 95 next to them. And so let's just briefly go through them and see if we can help identify, not the text but help sort out how the date system works. My first question would be: Do you know why the strictly confidential number 01 would have the 14 July 1995 date next to it and then that date is repeated under datum, 14, 7, 95, and if you know. If you don't remember, we don't want you to speculate or wonder but if you know why the date is there twice, I'd appreciate it, but --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir, and I also don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at this first one, then, which is in ERN last four digits 5314, we notice that this first conversation is at 0704 hours, then there is another conversation at 0750 hours, and then as we turn the page we get to 0850 hours. And then when we get to the next document, which is last four digits ERN 5317, sorry, 5316, we see the same heading up in the left but this time, as we've said, it's 02.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I hate to interrupt you but I think we can simplify it much, much, much more. I see that the last of these documents is one which carries the date 15, 07, 1995. Do you have also one from 13th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honour, but I decided it would confuse the issue so I didn't bring it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it would simplify the issue because you would have one or two of 13th July, one or two of 15th July, and you can leave all the others of 14th July and we won't need any explanation from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will dig that up, Mr. President. There is a couple of issues that I think you'll be interested in seeing as we go through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's another matter but it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Witness, if you could concentrate on this number 2 document that's got the 02 number on it, and it appears to be from your unit, according to that heading, and -- but this time we see CSB, SDB Tuzla, which we all know is MUP. And then we see -- we see that the intercepts are in all caps. Now I'd asked you yesterday if you recalled whether or not -- you said you recalled giving the MUP intercepts but we didn't talk in detail about the MUP giving you intercepts. Can you -- in looking at there, can you tell us what this report number 2 is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report number 2 is the -- a report by the SDB or DB as we call it from Tuzla which was sent to their unit via our computer. They were entitled to do so. This was approved by our command and they could do it any time, and I was not even in a position to know when they did that. And judging by this document, they indeed were using that service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But this went out with one of -- it went out with a 2nd Corps strictly confidential number on it, if this is correct. This has the appearance of a document that was sent to the -- by the army. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the upper title, where it says "the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," was sent from my computer. Everything under the line is the body of the text and it transpires from the body that it was sent by an SDB unit through our command. I suppose that their computer was out of order. This is just my assumption. And they were entitled to the right to send their reports through our computer. I did not even have to be informed about who the reports were sent to. The only thing that our operator would use would be a different heading containing the key for that day and then the material would be delivered. Another way one could do the same thing would be using a floppy disk that our operator could put in the computer to -- and send the report to the command of our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. One other thing on this front page, and you can read it. It's the -- and it's in English. It says, "VERY URGENT" in all caps. Do you understand what "very urgent" means in English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At least I can understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that something your unit used? Would you use English terms like this or is this an SDB term, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go back to everything above the line. This is the heading of my unit, which was part of the reports sent from our computer. Anything under the line is the SDB material. I was not familiar with their way of text processing. We used different ways of marking that something was urgent and the word that we used was "priority."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's just then go through the various dates. I don't need to go three each one of them. We see that 1 through 9 are all dated 14 July, and include various intercepts, but if we could go to number 9 which has got an ERN number of 03205330?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And looking up at that left-hand corner we see the usual heading, and we see the number 9, then we see that 14795 and under date it's 04, 01, 80. Now, can you explain how -- you know, how that might have happened or do you have any explanation? You mentioned problems yesterday. Any explanation for this glitch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't have any, but I said it yesterday that I know that there was some problem with regard the date and the key and I don't know what they did. If that was the case, then you should be looking for the person who could explain what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then if we continue to go through the conversations by number, we don't see any more misdates like that and then I want you to look at number 15. Do you see number 15? It is the ERN --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, isn't that the intercept that we were speaking of yesterday that was mentioning Major Jokic and Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's look at the next one, number 16, and it -- if you could. It's dated -- it has the numbers 14, 7, 95 on it. Do you see that? But then underneath that, under datum, it says 15, 7, 95. Do you have an explanation for that? What we see here is 1 through 16 with the 14 July 95 next to it but then now we have the date of 15 July underneath. Can you give us any help on the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I can see that in the heading there is a coded sign that you mentioned that has to do with the date, but that that code does not tally with the date. However, it transpires from the previous conversation, which was a priority, that that conversation took place at 2102 hours, which means that we kept on sending reports for that day but it was after 0000 hours, and that's why the date was different. In other words, a subsequent date was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, to look at this intercept itself we again see that it's CSB, SDB Tuzla, which has its own date on it of 14 July 1995. How does that tally with what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This shows that the material from the 14th was sent on the 15th. This material contains the material of the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to the next one, which is -- has that date again of 15 July at the bottom. This is an ERN number 03205345. And it's the 01. So it appears to be -- we now have started over. So this is the first one for the 15th of July as we see it. But as we look at the intercept itself, we see that it's at 2241 hours, pretty late in the day. So bearing that in mind, let's take a look at number 2 on the 15th. Again, it says number 2. It says 15 July twice. And that conversation is at 0554 hours, very early in the morning on -- well, on this document with 15 July on it twice. Now, going back to the first document, 01, dated 2241 hours, in your opinion, based on your knowledge and this -- and having this sprung on you, can you give us your opinion what date this intercept from 2241 was actually intercepted on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I think about it, sir. I wouldn't like to really be very categorical about it. This material was probably not sent on -- with the report of that day because it arrived too late so it was most probably sent on the following day, with the report of the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. May I ask a question at this stage which you can put to the witness? Say a conversation is intercepted at 22.41 hours on a particular day. Normal day. It's recorded, transcribed in handwriting. It's read out to the person who converts it then into printed format. How much time would normally elapse between the moment of interception and the moment it is ready for transmission to whichever office they were transmitting it? A message like this which takes -- it's two typewritten pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you understand that question? You play want to put it in the context of July 14th which was as you know what the events were on those days. In you could answer the President's question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Your Honour, the materials had to be sent as soon as possible, as soon as technically and physically feasible. The materials had to be intercepted and taken down and this is not always an easy job. So you can't really say it took us five minutes, two minutes or so on. So when priority was at stake, it had to be sent along as soon as possible, even if certain details were missed, for the sake of speed, and this is probably evident. As a rule, when combat operations were being carried out, the material had to be sent to the command in the form of a report as soon as possible. On the average, for a group of conversations, regular conversations, none of which were urgent, it would take up to an hour; for a single conversation, perhaps about 20 minutes to half an hour. If there was no urgency expressed by the command for the sending of the reports, the regular daily reports would be sent in the late evening hours, between 7.00 and 9.00 p.m. usually, and these would be regular reports when there were no combat operations ongoing. If there were combat operations, the situation would be different and we would send along a report as soon as we had it ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So as we looked at this packet with all these dates of 14 July and then moving on to 15 July, can you tell us, based on the process and the procedures, what dates these intercepts were actually captured and recorded on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From these documents, it's evident that the conversations were intercepted and recorded on the 14th and 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's set this thing aside and we'll remember to get the 13th so we have the other side of it, if you want it. I saw a head shake over there. So -- and let's go back to the documents that we were looking at before in Sanction but we need to make sure that they are not going out and I think we can still be in open session as long as the documents are going out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we will remain in open session but no broadcasting of the documents which we will be seeing on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record this is 65 ter numbers 1164 E. We should have the English and the B/C/S. This is back to the 14 July 1995 Beara-Jokic conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, we were going over this conversation to get a feel for how you -- sorry, how you did this. Are we -- is -- can you see that conversation in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't have it on my screen. Yes, now I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think we had left off, I think you'd identified -- well, as we go down the actual conversation, you identified the first B as Badem, I think then you said you didn't know the next line, who -- the next two lines, who that was, then the next B was Badem. And then we come to this P. Can you tell us from looking at this, you know, who the -- who the P means? What participant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, sir. Can we zoom in on this so I can see? It's Palma.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then we go to the next one, it's J and it says: "Hello, who is it, Major, I'm the duty officer at Palma, I need Beara urgently. This is Major Jokic. Who is that? Why the fuck are you not answering? Is Ostoja there? Is Brko there? Don't fuck around, the line has to be free and you must pick it up right away! Who is Ostoja? Is Ostoja there? Have him call me urgently. I will, I will. Hello! Hello!" Now, you've put J in front of that whole section. First of all, tell us who J is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: J is Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how do you figure out to put Jokic in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, those were the recommendations we were given, the gentleman introduced himself and I designated him as such, so he himself introduced himself. That's what we always did. That was our way of working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry to have to object at this point, Your Honour, but on the B/C/S version of this purported intercept, it doesn't say the words, "This is Major Jokic," as the Prosecutor clearly states so I think his questions are misleading and it's obvious the witness reading into that question says that he introduced himself. All it says is, "maj. Jokic". If he wanted him to say, "This is Jokic," he would have used the word "Ovo je Jokic" or "Majo Jokic," and he doesn't say that. He just says the words "maj." and then the name Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, if you look further down, on the English version, page 1, the very penultimate line, J: "Is that Beara? Jokic here." So when all this is transcribed, and the witness now knows because he's heard the speaker himself say, "Jokic here," he will put J next to what he believes is Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If he believes it's a different thing, Your Honour, but if he's been purportedly reading a translation of it that is significant in many parts, as we will see. I mean, if the courts wants to argue about it that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Know but it's.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's clearly misleading to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it is misleading because on the face of it the document itself indicates that this speaker described himself as Jokic. Of course, you can take this up on cross-examination in due course but it's a perfectly legitimate question. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a translation issue. This is a CLSS translation so it's not like I'm putting in, "This is" in this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sure you aren't. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, how do you -- you've got Jokic making all these comments, I take it. How do you -- how do you account for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were at least two possibilities for something like this to come up in the speech of one of the participants. First I have to explain to you the technical aspect of relay radio stations, FM-200 or RRU-800. Each of these relay stations including this multi-channel one had a transmitter and component. When we found a relay station we heard the participants who were on the transmitter side of the relay station best. Those are the ones we heard best. Very rarely or only occasionally were we able to monitor their incoming frequency. The other relay station that was linked up to them. So on one side, we heard one participant better than the other, and at the other end it was the other way around so that is a simple answer. Radio relay stations functioned differently than we hear them. They have the receiver component which we not hear through the pilot. This is sent on to the other side, and for this reason, it could happen that Mr. Jokic and the participant to whom he's talking either leaves very little space and we cannot hear the speech or we hear it but not well, and we could not capture that and transcribe it. But as there are no dots here, even if Astic [phoen] did hear something, I'm not going into that, we had very little space to put in dots to indicate that somebody is speaking here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there a possibly simpler explanation that Major Jokic was talking on two transmitters at once? He had one open trying to find Beara and he had a -- picking up another phone in the office trying to find somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I object to speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if you can answer the question without speculating, go ahead. If you can only speculate, then ask us not to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. I was only giving an example to show that a participant can say several sentences and at the same time be responding to someone else. Underneath you have a note, it's in very small print so I can't read it now but I know that it says here that a telephone line was open with one of the switchboards, and you can see which switchboard it is from the conversation itself. When this happened, Your Honours, it was easy to see how all this went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep going. We see B again, I take it that continues to be what, B?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Badem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then we have J for Jokic saying hello. And now we have X that says, I won't get into all of it but it's something about Snagovo and problems and Crni Vir. What's the significance of X when something like this you're hearing something like this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, sir, would happen in the situation I have just described. When X appears then there is an open line and we heard a participant who suddenly turned up out of no where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then we get another participant, Y, with "...". What's the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Y is a second unknown participant to whom person X was speaking, so we had several conversations going on here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you have no information or no words, how do you know there is a Y there and it's not just dead space?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, sir, if you heard a murmur or an indistinct conversation, we would put in dots. So anything that we were unable to transcribe in the form of words, we didn't even try to decipher noise that we couldn't actually tell what they meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then, let's go on. We have -- X makes another comment about the -- consolidating the lines. Then we have J, Jokic is back saying, "Hello." Then we have B, Badem, I guess, saying, "Just a moment. One moment old man." And then Jokic saying, "Is that Beara? Jokic here." And then we see the letters B and E, dot, dot, dot. What's -- what's that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: BE means Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how have you figured that Beara is in that conversation that you can't hear well because and then you've got dots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the course of the conversation, one can see that Mr. Jokic had already entered into conversation with someone and addressed him. And from the conversation he uses -- we can see that he later on uses his rank, he mentions it, and then we can see that Mr. Jokic is talking to the person he asked to talk to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we'll a little bit later go over the actual draft of the report to show how you decide when to put the various participants in, but let me ask you about that. Just -- well, we'll go over that when we get to the draft. Okay. So then we see Jokic saying, "We were together, Colonel, sir. Number 155 called you and asked to you call him urgently." Then the -- Beara cannot be heard. Then Jokic talks about Number 155, that means "... the higher house, you go ahead and call them, you have, so I don't speak like this." Then Beara can't be heard again. Jokic says, "Yes. Hey. We have huge problems over here." Beara can't be heard again. Jokic, "There are big problems. Well with the people, I mean, the parcel." Beara can't be heard. Jokic, "Who? Drago is nowhere around. I don't know where the others are all day." Again Beara can't be heard. Jokic says, "What? Call there [sic] number 155 in the higher house and that's it. OK boss." Beara, we have dot, dot, dot, and then for the first time, we have Beara with words, "Why number 155? Where is that?" Then Jokic responds: "Well, I can't tell you on this line, you know. You have it over there at the signalsmen, who that is." And Beara says, "Yes?" And Jokic says, "Bye." Again I don't want to you go through the whole explanation but can you tell us, do you have any opinion why, after not being able to really understand what Beara was saying, that you are able to catch the last two lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it's evident that the person at the switchboard was constantly switching on and off and manipulating the technology, that person was able to cut off the connection of the second participant or make it available, and that's the only assumption I can make, the only technical possibility of this happening, what we can see here, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that opinion is actually noted in the small remark at the bottom that where you say, "Thanks to a switchboard operator's mistake at Badem we recorded a conversation between X and Y who couldn't be heard while he was intercepting the line 44 was open for Jokic." How do you figure the mistake was at Badem and not at Palma?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the switchboard at Badem was switching Jokic on, opening the line, making it possible for us to hear Beara for at least a few moments. Everything was done by the participant at Badem. Excuse me, let me add something. And you can also see at the beginning of the text that Jokic is calling someone and I have to say, you see, you have the letter B up there. Each of the participants on one channel, on a multi-channel radio relay station, can also be heard on the small relay station but not necessarily. Also, one participant can be fixed, and this often happened. If this is contentious, we can investigate it further. But we would need the necessary documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to go to the actual notebook and copy of the notebook and look at the handwritten version as -- and ask you a bit how that came about and if we could get the original so I -- the Court may want to take a look at the court and it would probably be easier for the witness to look at it as well. I don't -- I know that counsel has seen it. I don't know if the Court wants to take a look?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have a hard copy of the document. What I suggest, however, if you require the witness to be in a better position, I think if you provide him with a hard copy, it will be better, and, of course, I don't know if it's the case of having it broadcast or not. That's another matter. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We shouldn't. There are some initials on the -- in the document. I think it would be best if the witness could actually have the original, we can put it on the ELMO. There is some colour in there that have some relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's better but we either do this then in private session, since there are some signatures, or else the understanding is that the -- what is -- appears on the ELMO is not broadcast. All right. Thank you. So there will be no broadcast of the document itself as it shows up on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the copy, the photocopy of this original is P02308 and if you could just hand him the original notebook, we'll just start out with some brief explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you take -- I know you've seen this before. Can you just start -- can you tell us what -- what this is as it fits into your testimony, briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the notebooks from my unit. They were used to transcribe conversations intercepted on relay radio stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said that there are some entries in colour. I think for that reason we need to see it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you start by just putting it on the ELMO just so we can see the front page, not the conversation yet but so that we can see the front page, and I think there are some numbers and things that I want to ask you about briefly. Yeah. The -- and I think we can -- there are some -- well, we all know that that vertical number is an ICTY number. And can you bring it down a little bit more so we can get the whole book on there, because there is a -- okay. It can't be seen very well but there is a number 9 up in the right-hand corner written. Do you have any idea who wrote that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for number 9, I don't know, and I also don't know anything about this bigger number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. How about the numbers a little bit below that or the letters. I see RRU and then something below that. Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my handwriting. This is radio relay device 1, which means that the notebook was to be used for transcribing material from the radio relay device number 1. This was the type of radio station, RRU-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about the number underneath it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number underneath is our number, the number in our unit. That's how we marked notebooks in my unit. They were numbered by numbers from 1 to 30-something, and this slash, Roman II, points to the fact that we also had a notebook number 29/I, and this is 29/II.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's open up the first page. And do you -- can you tell us, if you know, who wrote that and what it is, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text here is in my handwriting. This means that this is a book of reports for the radio relay device of this sort. Underneath this denotes the receiver, and the date is the date when the notebook started to be used, when the first entry was made, and we never put the date of the last entry into this notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you turn the page? I think on the left -- the left side there should be a little number, yeah, up in the left corner. Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was entered by the command, and it says, when the notebook was sent to us for our use. However, they did not have to send it on that particular date, but this entry denotes the date when it was entered in their books.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then let's go to the first page. Can we -- all right. Now, we've -- we see this and we see the -- what I think we've learned is the frequency and the time and participants. We don't see a date. And I asked but this last time but can you tell us, was the date normally put in these things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally it wasn't, because this was just a draft of the material that would later on become a document. I'm really sorry but this is how things were done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's flip through the notebook to ERN, last three digits 683.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could do that, usher, you'll see the ERNs in there. And if we could get the bottom half of the notebook, yeah, no, keep -- we need more of the bottom, sorry. Yeah, right there. Okay. That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, on this -- on this page of -- we -- above this, the time 0820 and I guess a frequency number, we see 12, 7, 95. Is that a date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could now just -- let's flip to the next page. We see that this conversation is at 0820 hours in a certain handwriting and we go to the next page. We come to a conversation that has 0957 hours. And to try to -- to save some time, I can tell you that, having gone through this notebook on that, it goes from 0957 to 1115, 1250, 1300, 1305, 1640. And then the next entry is 1236 and there is an entry at 1400. And then the next entry is at 1218, and then 1221, 1234, 1650, 1827, 2048, and then 2102 is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We couldn't follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm trying hard to follow but I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were supposed to be taking my word for that because it is a bit hard to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I wonder if the witness is following.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I did speed up but if -- I can slow that down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you -- could you just do what I did and try to follow the different -- the times and the reason I'm doing this is, can you, by looking at this, identify different 24 hour periods leading up to this intercept of 2102 hours, which is the intercept we've been talking about all this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm going to say something about this document that I'm looking at currently. I can see that the signature is there, the operator's signature is there, and in some conversations there is also the signature of the person who recorded the conversation. The second thing that I can notice is the fact that this notebook was designated for the RRU-1 frequency, and all the previous frequencies testified to that fact. In other words, they were all RRU-1. And all of a sudden you have frequencies RRU-800. There it is, the first one. There was 785, fifth channel, 1145 hours. At that moment, the two notebooks were nixed, the RRU-1 and the RRU-800, and he started entering the conversation that was taken from the radio relay station which was either RRU-800 or FMU-200. This is what I can see. I can also see the sequence of the times of the conversations as they were recorded, and transcribed, but I would not dare venture and say that this was all either on the same day or that there was a certain sequence of times up to that conversation that you have mentioned, which I currently cannot locate. And that I cannot do for the fact that the two channels were mixed up. However, judging by the handwriting of the operative who used a blue ballpoint pen and who signed the transcript means that he was working in that shift on the 12th of July 1995, and that he made a note of the time when this conversation took place. Then he changed the ballpoint pen and again the same person continued working.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me interrupt you. Fair enough. Can you give us an idea of how many books were in use on a -- like a busy day in July, on these dates? We know you have four sets, you got two men or more, if needed, but can you give us an idea of how many books might be in use on a busy day like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There should have been four at any one time, at the disposal of the operatives. Maybe they lacked a notebook at the time or one was full at that moment. Whatever I said would be just speculation on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Once a book starts getting used, will it continue to be used continuously or could it get set aside and not used for a day or two or more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could happen that it was set aside. Sometimes there was a mix-up and the notebook that should have been used wasn't used. This did happen. But all the notebooks were always there to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you -- if you've figured out our ERN number, do you see that big long number, let's go to the conversation we've been talking about, and it's 00779705 should be the first page of it. You see that in the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the Court's record, there should be a translation of the notebook version or handwritten version in your packet which is one of the explanations on why there is another translation. They are very similar, obviously, because the conversations are very similar but, as you can tell from the evidence, there may be slight changes so in this first one we have endeavoured to have two translations. And -- but actually it's not so much the English I'm concerned about here so let us -- can you put -- can we put this back on the screen again and perhaps just as a double effort, we can -- we can put -- yeah, we can put it on that screen, to Sanction, I guess. Okay. Could we put the original on the -- on the screen? Okay. Well, sorry, okay. We want that second conversation sort of in the bottom and we -- yeah. And we don't need the other page, if you could centre that conversation in there. Come up a little higher to get -- okay. Perfect. That's a good start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I think it comes through but do you recognise this conversation? Or do you recognise this handwriting, first of all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there any doubt in your mind you were the person that heard this conversation and transcribed it into the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: None whatsoever, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And just in looking at it, we see, like others, there is no date but it does start out with the frequency, channel, the time. And then we see next to the CH 3 and it looks like it's in -- well it is in blue ink from the original, and as is the X and the Y, is that your handwriting, the "PRIORITET" XY, in blue ink? And if you want to look at the original, you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting, sir. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know how it got there? Or do you have an opinion? I don't want you to speculate.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only people who knew about the conversation were myself and the person from the computer, the computer operator. Maybe you should ask him. Maybe he added this word, "PRIORITET," before I started reading this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who would have made the decision that it was a priority conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I was one who could have made that decision, but also we had a telephone link with the command and I could always get in touch with them and tell them that I had an interesting conversation, that a person from the OPP had called me and that they were interested to see it as soon as possible. And then the priority mode would be put in force and we would send it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, we can see somewhat on this screen that you have made various dark marks over -- and overwrites, or someone has, in this text. Can you take that pen and -- I think if you could -- and I know -- I know you've seen this before, but could you circle each little edit or correction for us, number it, and tell us what you think it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. What is he going to put his marks on, on the original or -- because I think what he has is the original notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, thank you, Your Honour. I meant the stylus on the computer so we are going to have so switch off from the ELMO to back to -- excuse me, to the other one. I'm -- a lot of balls in the air on this one. We need to call that up in e-court. Sorry, I've been working on Sanction and -- for him to mark it and it's worth, I think, calling the gods of e-court. And it's 1164B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As we are doing that, can you briefly tell us the process by which you would actually make marks on a draft like this? Why would you-- why would you make changes or marks, briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I can see in the text that in the course of the conversation itself, I noted Palma. However, when I continued listening in, probably as I was listening to the tape, although this is not important whether it was through the tape or through the conversation itself, all the new information was entered and the previous information was corrected. In addition to the original Palma, I added, "the duty operative at Palma." This was subsequently added. I also tried to enter a new participant, I gained more information, and that's when I added Major Jokic. And that's how the title came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go through each one of these things you're talking about, but let's start with the top and if you can get that -- if you can get that pen -- yeah, not the top conversation but the top of this conversation, which starts with "priority," and the first markover we can see is -- is right there, looks like next to -- next to Palma. Can you circle that and tell us what you think that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And put a 1 on that, will you and then tell us what you think it might be. Or what it is; we don't want you to speculate.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Since I am familiar with my handwriting, I will know what this is. This was E originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so you marked it over to put in what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually it was originally A, and then it became E.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So you changed it to an E, Palme?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then we see a -- another black mark on the next line down, by -- looks like something to do with "Bajru." Can you circle that, put a 2 on it, and tell us what you think you did there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Beara's name is here. There was something unclear here. I thought it wouldn't be legible so I repeated letter E in his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why did you need for this to be legible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did not need it to be legible. We needed it to be correct and to be read correctly. The fact that it is not neat doesn't really make a difference at all. Because this document was just a draft of the future real document. This is just raw material that had to be processed in a way, and while doing that, we were not supposed to change anything in the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- this is my last ten minutes but I -- I see it's break time. We just need to finish this up and I'll -- I'll be through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's make good use of the remaining ten minutes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, we still have that up on the screen. Could you go back to number 1 and right before the P in Palma, there looks like some words. Do you know what those -- what that word is and whether that was something you added or can you tell from your writing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that I added this subsequently. This is an abbreviation, DEZ, and that stands for duty officer Palma.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, let's go to the third change or addition or edit or whatever we want to call it. Can you go down this document and point to anything that you recognise as an edit and circle it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, sir. Let me try and find such things. [Marks]. I can see two dots below.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the -- this "Halo" here, for the first time we see the designation of the participant and a dash. As we listened to this conversation, we realised that this participant also says, hello and that's why the dots are bold. This was the simplest way of doing it, which means that the above text and the hello are attributed to the same participant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that second "Halo" is also Mr. J for Jokic in your final text; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If we can have the -- if we can continue with this document to keep going on it, it goes for -- the next page, I don't know if it's the next page or if we can just go up, I'm not sure how it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we can go to a next page before he puts his signature or his PW number on this page, because they come up separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then why don't you let him circle DEZ as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you circle DEZ that first thing you spoke of and let's give it a number next in order, 4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Yes, sir, I've just done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Go to the next page. And witness, you can always look at the original book, if you'd like, to help clarify things. Okay. From the top, do you see any -- any of your edits that -- can you circle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could have been a mistake in letters, maybe an attempt was made to write a word. In any case, it was a grammatical error, and in order to avoid any confusion, I blotted it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is letter B, which I edited. Originally, it was -- I wouldn't wish to speculate. I believe it was a P but I know that it was edited and changed into B. This is what I can see. And this happened when I listened to the sequence of participants in the conversation and I realised that the participant in question was neither Jokic nor anybody else but that it was somebody speaking at Badem, the switchboard operator at Badem said that. This is the same voice that I marked at the beginning as Badem, and this voice says, "Wait a moment." And it was not said by the person speaking before. I can tell from this transcript that this conversation was not easy to transcribe and that's why there are so many grammatical and other errors in this transcription. [Marks]. One more mistake, number 7, this is where I used small letters rather than capitals. I don't know whether immediately or later on, as I went through the text, I realised that it should be a capital letter and that's when I edited this original small letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me ask you to go up just below your circle 6. We see a large B and then a small letter E. Can you tell us anything about that? I think we remember what you said about it, about the conversation, but how about in the drafting? In looking at that and studying it, can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It transpires from number 6 that this was said by the switchboard operator and that this was -- this could be heard very well. And then he hands it over to somebody else whom I couldn't hear that well. Either I had noise in the headphones or something else, and I couldn't transcribe it. It transpires from the sequence of letters B and E that it was actually B that was speaking, and B stands for Beara [as interpreted]. He is the participant who was contacted by Jokic. And all these corrections only say that the conversation had to be listened to several times in order to be transcribed correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, which that little B, sorry that little E next to the large B, do you know if you added that later or was that something you wrote down at the same time you wrote the big B?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Not at the same time. I would not have done it that way. I would have written more neatly. I gave the name to this participant as I continued listening to the conversation, when Mr. Jokic named that participant and then when I listened to the conversation for the second time and then for the third time and I don't know how many times, that is when I realised how many participants there were in the conversation and then I could mark them, because originally, he was marked only as a participant at Badem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then, could you circle that first "Be," and that would be edit number 9?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you look down the rest of the -- the rest of the text and wherever you see a B small e that you added could you circle and number that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Do you want me to put the same number 9 next to every entry?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. I think we can just go in sequence but --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We need, I guess, is it a new page so we need to get it marked if we -- or can it be raised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it can be raised, yeah. I think it can be raised but -- no? Because as it is I think the moment it's zoomed in, it cannot be zoomed further in or out. So I think he has to put his PW number and move to the next or -- to the next part. Witness, could you kindly put in the same area where you have number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, do you see where you have written number 6 on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now on the right-hand side there is more or less an empty space between where you can put PW-132. Can you please try to put PW-132 -- yes. It's written here, can you save it again now? He's made PW-132 now. I think I know what I'm talking about. And we will discard the one you saved and we will have this new one. Okay? All right. So, gentlemen, and ladies, the understanding is that the previous one, which did not have the PW-mark on it will be discarded. It was saved but it will be discarded and we will save this one instead which will be the document to be tendered, okay? Understood? Okay. So let's have the same document now, go further down, possibly even zoom. Are we there, Mr. McCloskey, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we are. Maybe the witness remembers where he left off. We don't need to circle -- we didn't need to start all over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But if you can remember where we left off just continue doing the numbering for this capital B, little E --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, further down, that's it. Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think we are at number 15 -- 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 15 was the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I think we are on, what, 17?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll soon tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 16, sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. As far as I can remember, the last number I used was number 15 before this. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think there is a couple more you haven't circled but I don't have a photographic memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can always lend you mine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is where I know that I was missing space the first time when Beara spoke. I put number 15 because I was afraid that this could not be recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've confirmed it was number 15, the last number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Be that as it may, all the big Bs little Es, it's the same explanation basically; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to one last exhibit, 65 ter 1164, and we can save this, sorry, put your number on it again, we'll save this one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 1164D. Okay. Could we blow this up a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this is an intercepted document. We can see that it's the 2102 Jokic intercept that we have been talking about. This has been shown to you in a previous trial. You saw it in my office. Do you have any idea what this particular printout is, what unit it belongs to or how this came to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is -- was taken over by the unit of state security from us and handed it over to their unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I thank you so much, Mr. McCloskey. Now, who is going first? Mr. Zivanovic, who is appearing for Colonel Popovic, will be the first to cross-examine you. Take your time, Mr. Zivanovic. You indicated yesterday that you will require about an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Some of the questions that I intended to put have already been put on direct, so I'm sure that my cross-examination will last less time than I intended to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Thank you, and have a break at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me -- can we please go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
